path.id: Direct and Delegated Democracy Decision making and power rooted in communities, collectives, exercised in form of care, interbeingness, community rights and responsibilities, and respect for and kinship with all of life.
Ecological Integrity & Resilience Deep care for nature – protecting biodiversity, preserving ecological functions, and respecting the rights of all life, guided by ecological ethics in all actions.

Economic Democracy An economy that cares for all people and the rest of nature, never pushing costs to peripheries (offshore, downstream, non-humans, future generations). Local economies, commons-based exchange, a shrinking owner–worker gap.

Alternatives are different ways of doing things rooted in justice, care for the Earth, and shaped by people and communities. It could be a revived tradition, a new idea, or a quiet, everyday practice that challenges the dominant system. It’s not just about opposing what's wrong, it’s about building something better. A reimagining of how we live, decide, share, grow, and learn.

Alternatives nudges us to rethink the world we’ve accepted. It challenges the dominant system (based on capitalism, state domination, patriarchy, human-cent redness, etc) and moves us toward justice, sustainability, and collective well-being. Alternatives makes real shifts in key areas — they make meaningful changes to values, power, or relationships.
Alternatives take many forms, but they grow through five connected areas, like petals of a flower. The more petals touched, the deeper the transformation.
Ambadiba in South Africa: Commons based wealth and resistance
Deccan Development Society, India: Dalit Women Reclaiming Food, Land, and Autonomy

The Amadiba region in South Africa’s Eastern Cape is home to communities whose livelihoods are rooted in small-scale farming, fishing, and deep ties to land and biodiversity. All their land is held in the commons. Even after South Africa emerged from apartheid, private corporations, enabled by the state, began grabbing land and resources and dictating development policy.

The Deccan Development Society comprises of Dalit and tribal women farmers in the dryland regions of Telangana (India), where agriculture has long been shaped by caste hierarchies, land alienation, and ecological stress. Organised through village-level collectives known as Sanghams, women farmers came together to rebuild livelihoods rooted in millets, biodiversity, and collective decision-making. Over time, these Sanghams evolved into a powerful grassroots movement centred on food sovereignty, ecological regeneration, and women’s leadership.

For over two decades, communities have faced several proposals for destructive “development” projects, including titanium mining, oil and gas exploration in the ocean, urban expansion, and a proposed highway. These projects threaten biodiversity hotspots, community farmlands, and traditional livelihoods, while government institutions enable land grabs and do not seek community consent.

Mainstream agricultural development in the region promoted chemical inputs, monocropping, market dependence, and centralised food systems. These approaches undermined dryland ecologies, displaced traditional food cultures, and deepened the marginalisation of Dalit & tribal women farmers. Public food systems prioritised rice and wheat, ignoring millets that were better suited to local ecologies and nutritional needs. As a result, communities became dependent on external markets and state systems, while losing control over seeds, diets, and livelihoods.

The people of Amadiba insist that they are not “poor,” because their wealth lies in land, nature, mutual aid, and self-sustained ways of living that modern states have failed to recognise. Their struggle builds on a long history of resistance, in which women have played a central role, challenging not only the state but also patriarchy within their own communities.

Sangham women reframed development around autonomy, dignity, and ecological balance. Food was understood not as a commodity, but as the basis of culture, health, and self-reliance. Millets, once dismissed as “poor people’s food,” were reclaimed as central to local diets and farming systems. Decision-making shifted to collective forums where women determined what to grow, how to distribute food, and how to care for land and seeds. Development, in this view, meant strengthening local control rather than integrating into distant markets.

The Amadiba people are not simply resisting. They are actively creating alternatives rooted in agroecology, community-led ecotourism, and commons-based livelihoods. Their approach challenges privatisation and extractivism, placing solidarity, care, and the rights of nature and humans at the centre of well-being. They exemplify all the petals of the Flower of Transformation.

The DDS model represents an alternative because it replaces market-driven agriculture with community-controlled food systems. Seed sovereignty, collective farming, and non-monetary exchanges reduce dependence on external inputs and volatile markets. Community-run grain banks and alternative Public Distribution Systems prioritise local millets and nutritional needs over standardised state provisioning. By centring women’s leadership, commons-based resource management, and ecological farming, and by resisting GMOs and chemicals, the Sangham movement demonstrates that food security and wellbeing can be achieved outside industrial agriculture and corporate food regimes.

Through the Amadiba Crisis Committee, villagers, women leaders, youth, farmers, and fishers mobilised to demand the right to decide their own future. They used constitutional mechanisms, public mobilisation, alliances with national networks, and legal battles to stop destructive mining and exploration. They even rejected their own chiefs who aligned with corporate forces. The Amadiba struggle shows that genuine transformation does not come from state-led development, but from empowered communities reclaiming autonomy, direct democracy, protecting the commons, and relating to nature in kinship and spiritual terms.

This transformation emerged through sustained grassroots organising. Women formed Sanghams to pool knowledge, labour, and resources. They reclaimed fallow land, secured women’s rights to land, and revived biodiverse farming. Community seed banks protected indigenous varieties and reduced reliance on commercial seeds. Farmer–consumer initiatives created ethical relationships beyond conventional markets. Advocacy & national networking around millets influenced broader conversations on public food systems. All religious festivals were celebrated, centring seeds and earth as sacred. Change unfolded slowly, through trust, collective learning, and everyday acts of cooperation.
Kurdistan: Autonomy, ecology and feminism
Ladakh, India: Homestays & Community-Led Tourism

Kurdistan is a vast, war-torn region spanning Turkey, Iraq, Syria, and Iran, inhabited by Kurds alongside Armenians, Yezidis, Arabs, Christians, & other ethnicities. For decades, communities here have faced persecution, massacre, forced displacement, and sustained attempts to erase their cultural and political identities. Despite militarisation, invasions, and fascist attacks, hundreds of settlements have organised around women’s freedom, ecological living, and radical democracy.

Ladakh opened to tourism in the 1970s, and since then the number of visitors has from about 500 to 500,000! Much of this is concentrated within a short summer season. Trekkers and tourists passed through villages, often camping in open areas and moving on. While tourism was growing, most of the income went to hotels, travel agents, and transport operators based elsewhere. For many villagers, especially those living close to wildlife habitats, tourism brought little benefit and increasing pressure on land and grazing areas.

Nation-states that contain Kurd territories have imposed violent control through militarisation, cultural bans, forced assimilation, and the destruction of communal lands. Colonial legacies, capitalist modernity, and patriarchal structures have fractured social fabric, undermined ecological resilience, and denied communities the right to self-govern. Women and minority groups have been systematically marginalised within deeply hierarchical systems.

Communities observed that tourists came and left without engaging with local life. Garbage accumulated along trekking routes and near villages, and pack animals brought in for camping added pressure on already scarce grazing land. People living in remote settlements said they earned nothing from tourism except the burden of waste and disturbance. At the same time, livestock losses to wildlife such as snow leopards continued to affect livelihoods, reinforcing tensions between conservation and everyday survival. Tourism, as it was unfolding, did not support either village economies or care for the landscape.

Rather than seeking a nation-state, the Kurdish movement consciously shifted toward building radical democracy—direct, communal, confederal, and diverse. This shift emerged from confronting multiple, overlapping crises mentioned earlier, and from a realisation that another nation-state would only replicate patterns of domination they were trying to get away from.

During discussions by the NGO Snow Leopard Conservancy - India Trust in villages around Hemis National Park, women suggested a simple shift. Instead of tourists camping outside, they could stay in village homes. Hosting visitors would reduce the need for pack animals and camping gear, ease pressure on grazing land, and allow families to earn some income directly. It would also give visitors a chance to experience local food, culture, and daily life. With support from organisations working on wildlife conservation, this idea grew into a community-based homestay initiative rooted in shared responsibility and local decision-making.

Kurdistan’s movement, especially in regions like Rojava (Syria) where it has progressed the most, embodies the Flower of Transformation—ecological integrity, social justice, democratic participation, economic commons, and cultural diversity. Women’s liberation and the erosion of patriarchy are foundational, not peripheral. Gender equality shapes every political, economic, and social institution, offering a direct challenge to state-centric, top-down, and exploitative models of development.

Villages such as Rumbak began organising homestays collectively, with households taking turns to host guests. Women played a central role in managing bookings, preparing food, and coordinating income sharing. Tourists stayed with families, ate local meals, and learned about farming, livestock, and life in high-altitude villages. Income from homestays helped households meet basic needs and reduced dependence on seasonal migration. Villages also began collecting garbage along paths and setting up systems to manage waste. Part of the income was set aside for community use, including improving livestock protection and supporting conservation efforts linked to snow leopard habitats. Youth in many villages also got trained as nature guides.

Drawing on Kurd activist-ideologue Abdullah Öcalan’s philosophy of democratic modernity and confederalism, thousands of communes, assemblies, and cooperatives have been organised across Kurdistan. Women have emerged as leaders, educators, and theorists, building institutions such as women’s councils, Jineoloji academies, and cooperatives, while efforts are made to include diverse ethnicities in decision-making. Practices of collective education, self-criticism, cooperative economies, and ecological campaigns embed these values into everyday life. Even under conditions of war and repression, the movement demonstrates that transformation is possible by living alternatives. Through shared institutions, feminist politics, and ecological ethics, the Kurdish movement nurtures a pluriverse of just and sustainable ways of living, captured in its slogan: jin (women), jiyan (life), azadi (freedom).

The Ladakh homestay initiative shows how tourism can be reshaped through local priorities and everyday knowledge. By placing villagers (especially women) and nature at the centre, tourism became a source of livelihood rather than disruption. Staying in homes reduced environmental pressure, strengthened respect for local culture, and created a direct link between income and care for the landscape. The experience demonstrates that small shifts, grounded in lived realities, can bring genuine development, conservation, and community well-being together.
Communes in Germany: Collective living and sharing
Nagaland, India: Women-Centred Millet Revival

Within intensely capitalist, individualistic, and consumerist societies of the global North, small but inspiring experiments of collective, self-organised living are emerging in Germany. Communes such as Fuchsmühle, gASTWERKe, and shared living projects around Kassel demonstrate that comfortable and fulfilling lives can be lived with drastically reduced material and energy consumption. These communities pool spaces, resources, and labour, combining commons-based economies with solidarity, inner transformation, and democratic decision-making.

In many villages across Nagaland, millets were once central to farming, food, and everyday life. Grown alongside pulses, vegetables, and forest foods, they were part of biodiverse farming systems shaped by local ecology and seasonal rhythms. Women played a key role in seed selection, storage, cooking, and transmission of knowledge. Over time, changes in food habits, market pressures, and agricultural policies led to a steady decline in millet cultivation and consumption, even as communities continued to depend closely on land and forests for survival.

Dominant systems of capitalism, consumerism, and competitive individualism have generated ecological collapse, social isolation, and deep inequality. In their attempts to break these trends, communes face legal restrictions, cultural barriers from surrounding populations, and the overwhelming influence of market logic. Collective living also involves navigating interpersonal tensions, balancing individual and community needs, and competing with subsidised mass-produced goods.

As millets disappeared from fields and plates, villages became more dependent on a narrow range of crops and external food supplies. This reduced dietary diversity and weakened local food security, especially during climate stress and economic disruption. Traditional seed knowledge began to fade, and younger generations grew disconnected from crops their elders had relied on for generations. Women farmers observed that farming was becoming more input-dependent and less responsive to local conditions, while community control over seeds and food systems was slowly eroding.

These communes intentionally challenge high-consumption and individualistic lifestyles typical of industrialised societies. By centring commons, sharing, and solidarity, they show that moderate-consumption living can be both ecological and fulfilling. Through non-hierarchic decision-making, pooled incomes and resources (such as vehicles, washing machines, and kitchen space), community-supported agriculture, and freedom from market-based exchange logic, they create spaces that exist beyond capitalism.

Women farmers and community organisations, including the North East Network, began working to bring millets back into everyday cultivation and use. Rather than treating millets as a niche or commercial crop, they approached them as part of a larger effort to strengthen food sovereignty, revive indigenous knowledge, and restore ecological balance. The focus was on community control over seeds, shared learning, and reconnecting food with culture, health, and land.

Communes such as Fuchsmühle and gASTWERKe were created by pooling resources, restoring abandoned spaces, and building shared infrastructures including housing, kitchens, gardens, toolsheds, and childcare spaces. Decisions are made through sociocracy, plenaries, heart-rounds, and working groups, addressing emotional, practical, and strategic dimensions of community life. Shared budgets, collective care work, and non-exchange-based contributions recognise different forms of labour equally.

In villages such as Chizami and across Phek district, women established community seed banks to conserve indigenous millet varieties and other traditional crops. Seed exchanges and biodiversity festivals created spaces for farmers to share knowledge, stories, and farming practices. Millets were reintroduced into household diets and local markets, and community resolutions encouraged collective responsibility for seed conservation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, these local food systems proved crucial, helping families rely on their own fields when access to markets and wage work collapsed. Youth were also drawn into farming, documentation, and storytelling through films and community initiatives that reaffirmed pride in local practices.

Germany’s commune and solidarity-economy movements do not claim to have all the answers, nor are they yet strong enough to overcome dominant systems. Yet their growing presence shows that radically reduced consumption, deep community, and equitable sharing are not only possible, but can be more fulfilling than individualistic, capitalist-logic living. These “nowtopias” offer concrete imaginaries and practices for moving toward more just and sustainable futures.

The revival of millets in Nagaland shows how strengthening indigenous food systems can rebuild resilience from within communities. By valuing women’s knowledge, collective seed stewardship, and farming practices shaped by local ecology, villages restored both food security and cultural continuity. This work demonstrates that responses to climate uncertainty and economic vulnerability already exist in lived practice, and that sustaining them depends on respect for local knowledge, shared responsibility, and long-term care for land and community.
Zapatista Autonomous Communities in Mexico
Marudam Farm School, India: Experience-Based Learning

The Zapatista movement emerged in Chiapas, Mexico, out of histories of Indigenous peoples’ dispossession, land inequality, and political exclusion. In 1994, in response to neoliberal reforms such as North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), the movement gained global attention. Initially it involved armed self-defence. But soon it shifted from armed struggle toward building autonomous communities rooted in Indigenous traditions, collective decision-making, and dignity.

Marudam Farm School began as a small learning space shaped by the belief that children learn best when learning is connected to life. Located on organic farmland near Tiruvannamalai (Tamil Nadu), the school grew gradually, responding to the needs of children and families rather than following a fixed plan. The land, the people who live and work on it, and the everyday rhythms of farming became central to how learning unfolded. Children of different ages learn together, sharing space, work, and responsibility in a setting where education is rooted in place.

For the Zapatistas, the central problem was not simply poverty or lack of development, but the dominant development and political model itself. Capitalism and state-led development imposed a single vision of progress based on markets, money, and growth. This eroded communal land relations, undermined local knowledge, deepened inequality, and drove ecological degradation. Political representation in parties and governments offered little real agency, while economic policies & practices often deepened dependence on external institutions.

Many families and educators associated with Marudam felt that conventional schooling often reduced learning to classrooms, textbooks, and exams. Children were separated from nature adn community, physical work, and meaningful participation in daily life. Curiosity was frequently replaced by pressure to perform, and learning became something abstract rather than lived. For some children, this led to boredom, anxiety, or a loss of confidence. The question that emerged was how education could support the whole child rather than focus only on academic outcomes.

Zapatista communities reframed freedom as autonomy practiced in everyday life. Rather than seeking integration into markets or recognition from the state, they have prioritised self-determination, collective sufficiency, and direct participation. Decision-making takes place through assemblies guided by mandar obedeciendo—to lead by obeying the collective will. This shift rejects universal models of progress in favour of multiple ways of living well.

At Marudam, learning is closely woven into everyday activities on the farm. Children participate in growing food, cooking meals, caring for animals, building structures, and maintaining shared spaces. Academic learning arises through observation, discussion, experimentation, and creative expression. Teachers act as facilitators who learn alongside children, allowing interests and questions to shape the direction of study. Time outdoors, free play, storytelling, art, and collective work are seen as essential parts of education, not as extras. Valuable learning has also been centred around regeneration of forests on a nearby hill.

The Zapatista experience moves beyond reforming capitalism toward creating parallel systems outside it. Money and markets are decentered in favour of reciprocity, responsibility, ecological balance, and collective sufficiency. Well-being is defined through dignity, mutual care, and communities’ ability to decide their own futures. Governance is horizontal and rooted in consent, while resources are managed as commons. Substantive democracy and collective provisioning contrast sharply with state-centric, competitive election, and market-driven models.

A typical day at Marudam includes a mix of individual exploration and collective work. Children plant seeds, prepare compost, observe insects, and track seasonal changes on the land. Projects may involve mapping water flows, understanding soil health, or exploring local history through walks and conversations. Meals are prepared together using food grown on the farm, and shared responsibilities help children understand cooperation and care. Parents and community members are part of the learning process, contributing skills, stories, and time. Education here evolves slowly, shaped by relationships and experience rather than fixed schedules.

This alternative was built through sustained collective practice rather than policy interventions. Land was recovered and held in common; governance structures were developed through experimentation, and leadership roles rotate to prevent the concentration of power. Autonomous schools, clinics, justice systems, and media reflect local knowledge and needs, supported by solidarity networks without dependency. These practices show that autonomy is not just a future ideal but a lived reality, where communities satisfy basic needs within ecological limits, social justice and democratic control.

Marudam Farm School demonstrates that education can be grounded in land, community, and everyday life. By allowing children to learn through doing, observing, and relating, the school nurtures curiosity, responsibility, and a sense of belonging. Learning becomes meaningful because it is connected to real needs and real places. Marudam shows that alternative education does not require grand systems or rigid models, but careful attention to how children grow, learn, and live together with the world around them, and connect deeply with each other and with nature.
People’s Alternative Regionalism in Southeast Asia
Korchi Maha Gramsabha, India: Adivasi Self-Governance

Regionalism typically refers to formal cooperation across states in politics, economics, or diplomacy. In Southeast Asia, institutions like ASEAN focus on trade, investment, and elite diplomacy, but often fail to address democratic breakdowns, forced migration, ecological crises, and social exclusion. Communities across Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, Myanmar, Laos, and Vietnam experience interconnected struggles that cross state borders. People’s alternative regionalism emerges from these realities, seeing the region not as a market or a bloc but as a network of relationships shaped by culture, ecology, migration, and shared histories of resistance.

In Korchi block of Gadchiroli in central India, Adivasi (Indigenous) communities have lived with their own customs of governance, community custodianship over forests, and collective decision making. These practices have sustained livelihoods, protected ecological systems, and shaped social life for generations. Formal governance structures introduced from outside often did not reflect these lived realities or respond to community needs. People felt that decision making and well being were separated in practice, leaving choices about forests, land, water, and resources controlled by distant authorities rather than by the people who depend on them.

State-led regionalism prioritizes non-interference, stability, and economic integration. Capital, infrastructure, and extractive projects move freely across borders, while communities face displacement, repression, and precarity. Governments and formal institutions often fail to protect life, land, dignity, or democratic freedoms. Political repression, forced migration, climate disasters, and social inequality cross borders and affect communities in multiple countries simultaneously. People needed a form of regional cooperation that begins with those experiencing these challenges directly, not with intergovernmental treaties or elite diplomacy.

Official systems of democracy treated community members as passive recipients of policies rather than as active decision makers. Rights over forests, land, and natural resources were restricted, not accounting for local knowledge and customary practice. Women, in particular, found that formal processes excluded their voices even while they bore the daily responsibility for collecting water, tending fields, and keeping families safe. Many felt that democracy had become a slogan rather than a real practice and that wellbeing was defined in narrow, external terms rather than by people themselves. Additionally, the government was trying to impose inappropriate ‘development’ including mining in the area.

People’s alternative regionalism is grounded in care, solidarity, and everyday practices. It centers food sovereignty, indigenous knowledge, feminist organizing, mutual aid, and cultural exchange. It is based on ground-level practice, not only on theory. The region is already interconnected through shared ecologies, histories, and social networks. This form of regionalism is built not on agreements between governments but on relationships, trust, and shared responsibility amongst peoples across borders.

In response, villagers in Korchi began to reclaim governance through a broad based Maha Gramsabha (federation of village assemblies). This was a gathering of representatives (men & women equally) from 90 villages, chosen by their individual assemblies. It helped coordinate discussions & decisions on matters that affect community life. The Maha Gramsabha was a regular space for collective listening and deliberation. Everyone was encouraged to speak, especially women and elders, and decisions were taken through shared discussion rather than by a few leaders or external officials. The focus was on well-being in the fullest sense, including health, food, water, forests, education, and security of families and land.

Movements and communities connect through gatherings, seed exchanges, assemblies, cultural collaboration, and shared learning. In Cambodia, farmers in Trapang Svay protect land, save native seeds, cultivate collectively, and organise seed festivals, while communities in Phnom Krom and 78 Dam rebuild homes and sustain livelihoods despite repeated displacement. In Siem Reap, the APTBY LGBTQ Centre creates safe spaces where queer youth access mental health support and community care. Knowledge is treated as a commons, while cultural practices such as music, art, and rituals create a shared regional consciousness across borders. Everyday acts of care, solidarity, and mutual support form the infrastructure of alternative regionalism.

The Maha Gramsabha in Korchi organised its own committees to address core concerns of the village, and effectively resist mining proposals. Forest protection became a shared responsibility, drawing on their deep knowledge of seasonal cycles and species, strengthened by gaining recognition under the Forest Rights Act. Water resources were managed collectively. Women insisted on gender justice, raising issues of daily work, health, and safety. Village assemblies made decisions on land use, cattle management, school quality, and care for elders and children. These meetings became forums where people could listen to diverse views, shape solutions together, and guide collective action. Over time people found that shared governance strengthened their sense of dignity, reinforced mutual trust, and brought well-being into everyday life.

Alternative regionalism shows that regional futures can be shaped from below, through care, cooperation, and shared knowledge. Marginalized communities—farmers, displaced residents, women’s groups, queer networks—form the moral and political centre of the region. Institutions like MASSA’s People’s University aim to anchor lived knowledge as a regional commons, supporting cross-border learning and solidarity. This ongoing process demonstrates that hope, dignity, and collective responsibility can be woven across borders without relying on state-led integration.

The experience of the Korchi Maha Gramsabha shows that democracy centers the rest of nature can be reclaimed as a living practice rooted in community life. When people come together to listen, deliberate, and decide together, wellbeing becomes a collective project rather than an externally defined goal. Women’s voices gained space, local knowledge was respected, and decisions were grounded in the realities of the forest, water, and fields that sustain life. This form of self governance suggests that alternative visions of democracy are possible when they grow from relationships of trust, care, and shared responsibility in villages themselves.
Cooperation Jackson, USA
Homes in the City, Bhuj City, India

In an intensely racist context of exploitation and marginalisation of African descendants and other minorities in USA, Cooperation Jackson represents the struggle for democratic rights, economic justice, self-determination, and dignity for all workers. It helps mobilise workers in various sectors to assert their rights, gain collective power, establish and sustain dignified livelihoods, and challenge structures of inequity and injustice. In particular its work is amongst Black, Latino, unemployed, and poor residents. Amongst its main institutional responses is the formation of worker cooperatives and other worker-owned enterprises, drawing on a long history of such collectives in the Mississippi region. Its long-term objective is to transform Jackson and Kush settlements into dignified, humane, just spaces for people and nature to thrive.

Homes in the City (HIC) is an initiative in Bhuj, Kutch (Gujarat), started in 2015–16, that enables citizens to directly participate in Urban Local Bodies such as wards and the municipality. It brings together five civil society organisations working on water, gender, alternative building, biodiversity, and local governance. Building on the 74th Constitutional Amendment, the initiative supports citizens to form Area Committees (300–450 households), which nominate two representatives (a man and a woman) to Ward Committees (10–12 areas). It has been implemented in 5 of Bhuj’s 11 wards, largely among lower-income and marginalised communities.

Despite significant gains in policies and laws relating to civil rights and equality, there continues to be overt and covert racism in USA, combined with class, gender and other inequities. The urban poor suffer in terms of undignified, exploited work conditions, unemployment, and poor housing and civic services. In response, Cooperation Jackson is attempting to create a solidarity economy in which everyone can take part and benefit from, people’s assemblies in which direct democracy (communities on the ground being decision-makers) can be practiced, and pathways of collective care and mutual aid.

This initiative has enabled citizens to raise concerns with municipalities in a democratic way, including pressuring the government to expand a school facing severe space constraints. It has also led to initiatives such as Mahiti Mitras (information and service centres) that help people access rights and government schemes, women’s self-help groups (Sakhi Sanginis), and greater participation of women and girls in decision-making. Other efforts include resident-led affordable housing, restoration of a polluted wetland for safe water access, moves towards water self-sufficiency in a dry region, and the development of a ward-level Biodiversity Management Plan.

Cooperation Jackson has created cooperative institutions through which workers and residents generate dignified livelihoods in an urban context. A cooperative is an autonomous association of people who come together to meet shared economic, social, and cultural needs through a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise. These include a lawn care business, an organic farm, and a print shop, along with a cooperative incubator and a community land trust. Cooperatives in construction, housing, and waste management are also envisioned. Together, these initiatives address poverty and discrimination while remaining ecologically sensitive, and connect with wider movements challenging capitalism, racism, and other structures of domination.

This initiative has attempted to bring the true spirit of democracy alive in an urban context, wherein the currently dominant system makes most of the decisions in a highly centralized, bureaucratic, and top-down fashion. Typically, such top-down and elite-captured governance is at the cost of marginalized communities, who do not have much voice. This initiative gave voice to the people in the decision-making, leading to positive changes across many dimensions, such as gender equality, meeting basic needs such as water, housing, etc, and conservation of biodiversity. HIC has shown that in urban areas, all power need not be concentrated in elected politicians (corporators) and the bureaucrats they appoint, or in so-called 'expert' institutions, but that people can claim collective power to provide for themselves, as also make official agencies accountable.

In direct contrast to dominant systems that promote individualisation, selfishness, dependence on markets and governments, and hostile competition, Cooperation Jackson is based on values of self-help, self-responsibility, care, democracy, equality, equity, and solidarity. Members believe in honesty, openness, social responsibility, and care for others. They reinvest most of their surpluses into job creation, community development, and a social security system. The shift is from ‘I, me, mine’ to ‘We, us, ours’, without erasing individual identities. This extends to solidarity with oppressed peoples elsewhere, including raising funds for a greenhouse project in Palestine.

While the initiative led to many positive outcomes, challenges remained. Some corporators were less invested in their wards, and it was often difficult to sustain regular participation in Area Committee meetings beyond annual planning. Discussions tended to focus on immediate, local concerns rather than a broader vision for the wards. Meetings also prioritised infrastructure issues such as water and sanitation, while “softer” concerns like education, livelihoods, and mobility received less attention. This reflects a long-standing discourse that frames development primarily in terms of physical infrastructure rather than social transformation.

Cooperation Jackson shows us that it is possible to move towards dignity and humane living even in the face of intense exploitation and inequality. To do this, several factors are crucial: coming together as collectives, enabling the voice and agency of the marginalised, dreaming alternative futures with feet firmly rooted on the ground, networking with other movements, and trying new approaches knowing that some may fail. It is also important to have diverse activities such as practical economic activities, dialogues and workshops, events of mutual aid and care, celebratory events including art, music and festivals, demonstrations and solidarity protests, and more. Finally, Cooperation Jackson also displays the necessity of networking with other movements and groups across the region and globally, for cross-learning and collective strength.

This initiative shows that when citizens and CSOs come together, they can create a deeper and more holistic form of democracy, with communities at the centre of decision-making and representatives accountable to their needs. It brings local knowledge, innovation, and agency to the forefront rather than marginalising them. It also demonstrates that with the right opportunities, marginalised urban communities can assert themselves and move towards greater dignity and self-help. At a time of increasing centralisation, this offers hope for more decentralised forms of local governance in cities.
Looking at lived examples helps us understand how alternatives emerge, take root, and grow through everyday practice and collective action.

it’s a dog eat dog world_2

Alternatives are different ways of doing things rooted in justice, care for the Earth, and shaped by people and communities. It could be a revived tradition, a new idea, or a quiet, everyday practice that challenges the dominant system. It’s not just about opposing what's wrong, it’s about building something better. A reimagining of how we live, decide, share, grow, and learn._2

Alternatives nudges us to rethink the world we’ve accepted. It challenges the dominant system (based on capitalism, state domination, patriarchy, human-cent redness, etc) and moves us toward justice, sustainability, and collective well-being. Alternatives makes real shifts in key areas — they make meaningful changes to values, power, or relationships._2
Alternatives take many forms, but they grow through five connected areas, like petals of a flower. The more petals touched, the deeper the transformation._2
Ambadiba in South Africa: Commons based wealth and resistance_2
Deccan Development Society, India: Dalit Women Reclaiming Food, Land, and Autonomy_2

The Amadiba region in South Africa’s Eastern Cape is home to communities whose livelihoods are rooted in small-scale farming, fishing, and deep ties to land and biodiversity. All their land is held in the commons. Even after South Africa emerged from apartheid, private corporations, enabled by the state, began grabbing land and resources and dictating development policy._2

The Deccan Development Society comprises of Dalit and tribal women farmers in the dryland regions of Telangana (India), where agriculture has long been shaped by caste hierarchies, land alienation, and ecological stress. Organised through village-level collectives known as Sanghams, women farmers came together to rebuild livelihoods rooted in millets, biodiversity, and collective decision-making. Over time, these Sanghams evolved into a powerful grassroots movement centred on food sovereignty, ecological regeneration, and women’s leadership._2

For over two decades, communities have faced several proposals for destructive “development” projects, including titanium mining, oil and gas exploration in the ocean, urban expansion, and a proposed highway. These projects threaten biodiversity hotspots, community farmlands, and traditional livelihoods, while government institutions enable land grabs and do not seek community consent._2

Mainstream agricultural development in the region promoted chemical inputs, monocropping, market dependence, and centralised food systems. These approaches undermined dryland ecologies, displaced traditional food cultures, and deepened the marginalisation of Dalit & tribal women farmers. Public food systems prioritised rice and wheat, ignoring millets that were better suited to local ecologies and nutritional needs. As a result, communities became dependent on external markets and state systems, while losing control over seeds, diets, and livelihoods._2

The people of Amadiba insist that they are not “poor,” because their wealth lies in land, nature, mutual aid, and self-sustained ways of living that modern states have failed to recognise. Their struggle builds on a long history of resistance, in which women have played a central role, challenging not only the state but also patriarchy within their own communities._2

Sangham women reframed development around autonomy, dignity, and ecological balance. Food was understood not as a commodity, but as the basis of culture, health, and self-reliance. Millets, once dismissed as “poor people’s food,” were reclaimed as central to local diets and farming systems. Decision-making shifted to collective forums where women determined what to grow, how to distribute food, and how to care for land and seeds. Development, in this view, meant strengthening local control rather than integrating into distant markets._2

The Amadiba people are not simply resisting. They are actively creating alternatives rooted in agroecology, community-led ecotourism, and commons-based livelihoods. Their approach challenges privatisation and extractivism, placing solidarity, care, and the rights of nature and humans at the centre of well-being. They exemplify all the petals of the Flower of Transformation._2

The DDS model represents an alternative because it replaces market-driven agriculture with community-controlled food systems. Seed sovereignty, collective farming, and non-monetary exchanges reduce dependence on external inputs and volatile markets. Community-run grain banks and alternative Public Distribution Systems prioritise local millets and nutritional needs over standardised state provisioning. By centring women’s leadership, commons-based resource management, and ecological farming, and by resisting GMOs and chemicals, the Sangham movement demonstrates that food security and wellbeing can be achieved outside industrial agriculture and corporate food regimes._2

Through the Amadiba Crisis Committee, villagers, women leaders, youth, farmers, and fishers mobilised to demand the right to decide their own future. They used constitutional mechanisms, public mobilisation, alliances with national networks, and legal battles to stop destructive mining and exploration. They even rejected their own chiefs who aligned with corporate forces. The Amadiba struggle shows that genuine transformation does not come from state-led development, but from empowered communities reclaiming autonomy, direct democracy, protecting the commons, and relating to nature in kinship and spiritual terms._2

This transformation emerged through sustained grassroots organising. Women formed Sanghams to pool knowledge, labour, and resources. They reclaimed fallow land, secured women’s rights to land, and revived biodiverse farming. Community seed banks protected indigenous varieties and reduced reliance on commercial seeds. Farmer–consumer initiatives created ethical relationships beyond conventional markets. Advocacy & national networking around millets influenced broader conversations on public food systems. All religious festivals were celebrated, centring seeds and earth as sacred. Change unfolded slowly, through trust, collective learning, and everyday acts of cooperation._2
Kurdistan: Autonomy, ecology and feminism_2
Ladakh, India: Homestays & Community-Led Tourism_2

Kurdistan is a vast, war-torn region spanning Turkey, Iraq, Syria, and Iran, inhabited by Kurds alongside Armenians, Yezidis, Arabs, Christians, & other ethnicities. For decades, communities here have faced persecution, massacre, forced displacement, and sustained attempts to erase their cultural and political identities. Despite militarisation, invasions, and fascist attacks, hundreds of settlements have organised around women’s freedom, ecological living, and radical democracy._2

Ladakh opened to tourism in the 1970s, and since then the number of visitors has from about 500 to 500,000! Much of this is concentrated within a short summer season. Trekkers and tourists passed through villages, often camping in open areas and moving on. While tourism was growing, most of the income went to hotels, travel agents, and transport operators based elsewhere. For many villagers, especially those living close to wildlife habitats, tourism brought little benefit and increasing pressure on land and grazing areas._2

Nation-states that contain Kurd territories have imposed violent control through militarisation, cultural bans, forced assimilation, and the destruction of communal lands. Colonial legacies, capitalist modernity, and patriarchal structures have fractured social fabric, undermined ecological resilience, and denied communities the right to self-govern. Women and minority groups have been systematically marginalised within deeply hierarchical systems._2

Communities observed that tourists came and left without engaging with local life. Garbage accumulated along trekking routes and near villages, and pack animals brought in for camping added pressure on already scarce grazing land. People living in remote settlements said they earned nothing from tourism except the burden of waste and disturbance. At the same time, livestock losses to wildlife such as snow leopards continued to affect livelihoods, reinforcing tensions between conservation and everyday survival. Tourism, as it was unfolding, did not support either village economies or care for the landscape._2

Rather than seeking a nation-state, the Kurdish movement consciously shifted toward building radical democracy—direct, communal, confederal, and diverse. This shift emerged from confronting multiple, overlapping crises mentioned earlier, and from a realisation that another nation-state would only replicate patterns of domination they were trying to get away from._2

During discussions by the NGO Snow Leopard Conservancy - India Trust in villages around Hemis National Park, women suggested a simple shift. Instead of tourists camping outside, they could stay in village homes. Hosting visitors would reduce the need for pack animals and camping gear, ease pressure on grazing land, and allow families to earn some income directly. It would also give visitors a chance to experience local food, culture, and daily life. With support from organisations working on wildlife conservation, this idea grew into a community-based homestay initiative rooted in shared responsibility and local decision-making._2

Kurdistan’s movement, especially in regions like Rojava (Syria) where it has progressed the most, embodies the Flower of Transformation—ecological integrity, social justice, democratic participation, economic commons, and cultural diversity. Women’s liberation and the erosion of patriarchy are foundational, not peripheral. Gender equality shapes every political, economic, and social institution, offering a direct challenge to state-centric, top-down, and exploitative models of development._2

Villages such as Rumbak began organising homestays collectively, with households taking turns to host guests. Women played a central role in managing bookings, preparing food, and coordinating income sharing. Tourists stayed with families, ate local meals, and learned about farming, livestock, and life in high-altitude villages. Income from homestays helped households meet basic needs and reduced dependence on seasonal migration. Villages also began collecting garbage along paths and setting up systems to manage waste. Part of the income was set aside for community use, including improving livestock protection and supporting conservation efforts linked to snow leopard habitats. Youth in many villages also got trained as nature guides._2

Drawing on Kurd activist-ideologue Abdullah Öcalan’s philosophy of democratic modernity and confederalism, thousands of communes, assemblies, and cooperatives have been organised across Kurdistan. Women have emerged as leaders, educators, and theorists, building institutions such as women’s councils, Jineoloji academies, and cooperatives, while efforts are made to include diverse ethnicities in decision-making. Practices of collective education, self-criticism, cooperative economies, and ecological campaigns embed these values into everyday life. Even under conditions of war and repression, the movement demonstrates that transformation is possible by living alternatives. Through shared institutions, feminist politics, and ecological ethics, the Kurdish movement nurtures a pluriverse of just and sustainable ways of living, captured in its slogan: jin (women), jiyan (life), azadi (freedom)._2

The Ladakh homestay initiative shows how tourism can be reshaped through local priorities and everyday knowledge. By placing villagers (especially women) and nature at the centre, tourism became a source of livelihood rather than disruption. Staying in homes reduced environmental pressure, strengthened respect for local culture, and created a direct link between income and care for the landscape. The experience demonstrates that small shifts, grounded in lived realities, can bring genuine development, conservation, and community well-being together._2
Communes in Germany: Collective living and sharing_2
Nagaland, India: Women-Centred Millet Revival_2

Within intensely capitalist, individualistic, and consumerist societies of the global North, small but inspiring experiments of collective, self-organised living are emerging in Germany. Communes such as Fuchsmühle, gASTWERKe, and shared living projects around Kassel demonstrate that comfortable and fulfilling lives can be lived with drastically reduced material and energy consumption. These communities pool spaces, resources, and labour, combining commons-based economies with solidarity, inner transformation, and democratic decision-making._2

In many villages across Nagaland, millets were once central to farming, food, and everyday life. Grown alongside pulses, vegetables, and forest foods, they were part of biodiverse farming systems shaped by local ecology and seasonal rhythms. Women played a key role in seed selection, storage, cooking, and transmission of knowledge. Over time, changes in food habits, market pressures, and agricultural policies led to a steady decline in millet cultivation and consumption, even as communities continued to depend closely on land and forests for survival._2

Dominant systems of capitalism, consumerism, and competitive individualism have generated ecological collapse, social isolation, and deep inequality. In their attempts to break these trends, communes face legal restrictions, cultural barriers from surrounding populations, and the overwhelming influence of market logic. Collective living also involves navigating interpersonal tensions, balancing individual and community needs, and competing with subsidised mass-produced goods._2

As millets disappeared from fields and plates, villages became more dependent on a narrow range of crops and external food supplies. This reduced dietary diversity and weakened local food security, especially during climate stress and economic disruption. Traditional seed knowledge began to fade, and younger generations grew disconnected from crops their elders had relied on for generations. Women farmers observed that farming was becoming more input-dependent and less responsive to local conditions, while community control over seeds and food systems was slowly eroding._2

These communes intentionally challenge high-consumption and individualistic lifestyles typical of industrialised societies. By centring commons, sharing, and solidarity, they show that moderate-consumption living can be both ecological and fulfilling. Through non-hierarchic decision-making, pooled incomes and resources (such as vehicles, washing machines, and kitchen space), community-supported agriculture, and freedom from market-based exchange logic, they create spaces that exist beyond capitalism._2

Women farmers and community organisations, including the North East Network, began working to bring millets back into everyday cultivation and use. Rather than treating millets as a niche or commercial crop, they approached them as part of a larger effort to strengthen food sovereignty, revive indigenous knowledge, and restore ecological balance. The focus was on community control over seeds, shared learning, and reconnecting food with culture, health, and land._2

Communes such as Fuchsmühle and gASTWERKe were created by pooling resources, restoring abandoned spaces, and building shared infrastructures including housing, kitchens, gardens, toolsheds, and childcare spaces. Decisions are made through sociocracy, plenaries, heart-rounds, and working groups, addressing emotional, practical, and strategic dimensions of community life. Shared budgets, collective care work, and non-exchange-based contributions recognise different forms of labour equally._2

In villages such as Chizami and across Phek district, women established community seed banks to conserve indigenous millet varieties and other traditional crops. Seed exchanges and biodiversity festivals created spaces for farmers to share knowledge, stories, and farming practices. Millets were reintroduced into household diets and local markets, and community resolutions encouraged collective responsibility for seed conservation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, these local food systems proved crucial, helping families rely on their own fields when access to markets and wage work collapsed. Youth were also drawn into farming, documentation, and storytelling through films and community initiatives that reaffirmed pride in local practices._2

Germany’s commune and solidarity-economy movements do not claim to have all the answers, nor are they yet strong enough to overcome dominant systems. Yet their growing presence shows that radically reduced consumption, deep community, and equitable sharing are not only possible, but can be more fulfilling than individualistic, capitalist-logic living. These “nowtopias” offer concrete imaginaries and practices for moving toward more just and sustainable futures._2

The revival of millets in Nagaland shows how strengthening indigenous food systems can rebuild resilience from within communities. By valuing women’s knowledge, collective seed stewardship, and farming practices shaped by local ecology, villages restored both food security and cultural continuity. This work demonstrates that responses to climate uncertainty and economic vulnerability already exist in lived practice, and that sustaining them depends on respect for local knowledge, shared responsibility, and long-term care for land and community._2
Zapatista Autonomous Communities in Mexico_2
Marudam Farm School, India: Experience-Based Learning_2

The Zapatista movement emerged in Chiapas, Mexico, out of histories of Indigenous peoples’ dispossession, land inequality, and political exclusion. In 1994, in response to neoliberal reforms such as North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), the movement gained global attention. Initially it involved armed self-defence. But soon it shifted from armed struggle toward building autonomous communities rooted in Indigenous traditions, collective decision-making, and dignity._2

Marudam Farm School began as a small learning space shaped by the belief that children learn best when learning is connected to life. Located on organic farmland near Tiruvannamalai (Tamil Nadu), the school grew gradually, responding to the needs of children and families rather than following a fixed plan. The land, the people who live and work on it, and the everyday rhythms of farming became central to how learning unfolded. Children of different ages learn together, sharing space, work, and responsibility in a setting where education is rooted in place._2

For the Zapatistas, the central problem was not simply poverty or lack of development, but the dominant development and political model itself. Capitalism and state-led development imposed a single vision of progress based on markets, money, and growth. This eroded communal land relations, undermined local knowledge, deepened inequality, and drove ecological degradation. Political representation in parties and governments offered little real agency, while economic policies & practices often deepened dependence on external institutions._2

Many families and educators associated with Marudam felt that conventional schooling often reduced learning to classrooms, textbooks, and exams. Children were separated from nature adn community, physical work, and meaningful participation in daily life. Curiosity was frequently replaced by pressure to perform, and learning became something abstract rather than lived. For some children, this led to boredom, anxiety, or a loss of confidence. The question that emerged was how education could support the whole child rather than focus only on academic outcomes._2

Zapatista communities reframed freedom as autonomy practiced in everyday life. Rather than seeking integration into markets or recognition from the state, they have prioritised self-determination, collective sufficiency, and direct participation. Decision-making takes place through assemblies guided by mandar obedeciendo—to lead by obeying the collective will. This shift rejects universal models of progress in favour of multiple ways of living well._2

At Marudam, learning is closely woven into everyday activities on the farm. Children participate in growing food, cooking meals, caring for animals, building structures, and maintaining shared spaces. Academic learning arises through observation, discussion, experimentation, and creative expression. Teachers act as facilitators who learn alongside children, allowing interests and questions to shape the direction of study. Time outdoors, free play, storytelling, art, and collective work are seen as essential parts of education, not as extras. Valuable learning has also been centred around regeneration of forests on a nearby hill._2

The Zapatista experience moves beyond reforming capitalism toward creating parallel systems outside it. Money and markets are decentered in favour of reciprocity, responsibility, ecological balance, and collective sufficiency. Well-being is defined through dignity, mutual care, and communities’ ability to decide their own futures. Governance is horizontal and rooted in consent, while resources are managed as commons. Substantive democracy and collective provisioning contrast sharply with state-centric, competitive election, and market-driven models._2

A typical day at Marudam includes a mix of individual exploration and collective work. Children plant seeds, prepare compost, observe insects, and track seasonal changes on the land. Projects may involve mapping water flows, understanding soil health, or exploring local history through walks and conversations. Meals are prepared together using food grown on the farm, and shared responsibilities help children understand cooperation and care. Parents and community members are part of the learning process, contributing skills, stories, and time. Education here evolves slowly, shaped by relationships and experience rather than fixed schedules._2

This alternative was built through sustained collective practice rather than policy interventions. Land was recovered and held in common; governance structures were developed through experimentation, and leadership roles rotate to prevent the concentration of power. Autonomous schools, clinics, justice systems, and media reflect local knowledge and needs, supported by solidarity networks without dependency. These practices show that autonomy is not just a future ideal but a lived reality, where communities satisfy basic needs within ecological limits, social justice and democratic control._2

Marudam Farm School demonstrates that education can be grounded in land, community, and everyday life. By allowing children to learn through doing, observing, and relating, the school nurtures curiosity, responsibility, and a sense of belonging. Learning becomes meaningful because it is connected to real needs and real places. Marudam shows that alternative education does not require grand systems or rigid models, but careful attention to how children grow, learn, and live together with the world around them, and connect deeply with each other and with nature._2
People’s Alternative Regionalism in Southeast Asia_2
Korchi Maha Gramsabha, India: Adivasi Self-Governance_2

Regionalism typically refers to formal cooperation across states in politics, economics, or diplomacy. In Southeast Asia, institutions like ASEAN focus on trade, investment, and elite diplomacy, but often fail to address democratic breakdowns, forced migration, ecological crises, and social exclusion. Communities across Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, Myanmar, Laos, and Vietnam experience interconnected struggles that cross state borders. People’s alternative regionalism emerges from these realities, seeing the region not as a market or a bloc but as a network of relationships shaped by culture, ecology, migration, and shared histories of resistance._2

In Korchi block of Gadchiroli in central India, Adivasi (Indigenous) communities have lived with their own customs of governance, community custodianship over forests, and collective decision making. These practices have sustained livelihoods, protected ecological systems, and shaped social life for generations. Formal governance structures introduced from outside often did not reflect these lived realities or respond to community needs. People felt that decision making and well being were separated in practice, leaving choices about forests, land, water, and resources controlled by distant authorities rather than by the people who depend on them._2

State-led regionalism prioritizes non-interference, stability, and economic integration. Capital, infrastructure, and extractive projects move freely across borders, while communities face displacement, repression, and precarity. Governments and formal institutions often fail to protect life, land, dignity, or democratic freedoms. Political repression, forced migration, climate disasters, and social inequality cross borders and affect communities in multiple countries simultaneously. People needed a form of regional cooperation that begins with those experiencing these challenges directly, not with intergovernmental treaties or elite diplomacy._2

Official systems of democracy treated community members as passive recipients of policies rather than as active decision makers. Rights over forests, land, and natural resources were restricted, not accounting for local knowledge and customary practice. Women, in particular, found that formal processes excluded their voices even while they bore the daily responsibility for collecting water, tending fields, and keeping families safe. Many felt that democracy had become a slogan rather than a real practice and that wellbeing was defined in narrow, external terms rather than by people themselves. Additionally, the government was trying to impose inappropriate ‘development’ including mining in the area._2

People’s alternative regionalism is grounded in care, solidarity, and everyday practices. It centers food sovereignty, indigenous knowledge, feminist organizing, mutual aid, and cultural exchange. It is based on ground-level practice, not only on theory. The region is already interconnected through shared ecologies, histories, and social networks. This form of regionalism is built not on agreements between governments but on relationships, trust, and shared responsibility amongst peoples across borders._2

In response, villagers in Korchi began to reclaim governance through a broad based Maha Gramsabha (federation of village assemblies). This was a gathering of representatives (men & women equally) from 90 villages, chosen by their individual assemblies. It helped coordinate discussions & decisions on matters that affect community life. The Maha Gramsabha was a regular space for collective listening and deliberation. Everyone was encouraged to speak, especially women and elders, and decisions were taken through shared discussion rather than by a few leaders or external officials. The focus was on well-being in the fullest sense, including health, food, water, forests, education, and security of families and land._2

Movements and communities connect through gatherings, seed exchanges, assemblies, cultural collaboration, and shared learning. In Cambodia, farmers in Trapang Svay protect land, save native seeds, cultivate collectively, and organise seed festivals, while communities in Phnom Krom and 78 Dam rebuild homes and sustain livelihoods despite repeated displacement. In Siem Reap, the APTBY LGBTQ Centre creates safe spaces where queer youth access mental health support and community care. Knowledge is treated as a commons, while cultural practices such as music, art, and rituals create a shared regional consciousness across borders. Everyday acts of care, solidarity, and mutual support form the infrastructure of alternative regionalism._2

The Maha Gramsabha in Korchi organised its own committees to address core concerns of the village, and effectively resist mining proposals. Forest protection became a shared responsibility, drawing on their deep knowledge of seasonal cycles and species, strengthened by gaining recognition under the Forest Rights Act. Water resources were managed collectively. Women insisted on gender justice, raising issues of daily work, health, and safety. Village assemblies made decisions on land use, cattle management, school quality, and care for elders and children. These meetings became forums where people could listen to diverse views, shape solutions together, and guide collective action. Over time people found that shared governance strengthened their sense of dignity, reinforced mutual trust, and brought well-being into everyday life._2

Alternative regionalism shows that regional futures can be shaped from below, through care, cooperation, and shared knowledge. Marginalized communities—farmers, displaced residents, women’s groups, queer networks—form the moral and political centre of the region. Institutions like MASSA’s People’s University aim to anchor lived knowledge as a regional commons, supporting cross-border learning and solidarity. This ongoing process demonstrates that hope, dignity, and collective responsibility can be woven across borders without relying on state-led integration._2

The experience of the Korchi Maha Gramsabha shows that democracy centers the rest of nature can be reclaimed as a living practice rooted in community life. When people come together to listen, deliberate, and decide together, wellbeing becomes a collective project rather than an externally defined goal. Women’s voices gained space, local knowledge was respected, and decisions were grounded in the realities of the forest, water, and fields that sustain life. This form of self governance suggests that alternative visions of democracy are possible when they grow from relationships of trust, care, and shared responsibility in villages themselves._2
Cooperation Jackson, USA_2
Homes in the City, Bhuj City, India_2

In an intensely racist context of exploitation and marginalisation of African descendants and other minorities in USA, Cooperation Jackson represents the struggle for democratic rights, economic justice, self-determination, and dignity for all workers. It helps mobilise workers in various sectors to assert their rights, gain collective power, establish and sustain dignified livelihoods, and challenge structures of inequity and injustice. In particular its work is amongst Black, Latino, unemployed, and poor residents. Amongst its main institutional responses is the formation of worker cooperatives and other worker-owned enterprises, drawing on a long history of such collectives in the Mississippi region. Its long-term objective is to transform Jackson and Kush settlements into dignified, humane, just spaces for people and nature to thrive._2

Homes in the City (HIC) is an initiative in Bhuj, Kutch (Gujarat), started in 2015–16, that enables citizens to directly participate in Urban Local Bodies such as wards and the municipality. It brings together five civil society organisations working on water, gender, alternative building, biodiversity, and local governance. Building on the 74th Constitutional Amendment, the initiative supports citizens to form Area Committees (300–450 households), which nominate two representatives (a man and a woman) to Ward Committees (10–12 areas). It has been implemented in 5 of Bhuj’s 11 wards, largely among lower-income and marginalised communities._2

Despite significant gains in policies and laws relating to civil rights and equality, there continues to be overt and covert racism in USA, combined with class, gender and other inequities. The urban poor suffer in terms of undignified, exploited work conditions, unemployment, and poor housing and civic services. In response, Cooperation Jackson is attempting to create a solidarity economy in which everyone can take part and benefit from, people’s assemblies in which direct democracy (communities on the ground being decision-makers) can be practiced, and pathways of collective care and mutual aid._2

This initiative has enabled citizens to raise concerns with municipalities in a democratic way, including pressuring the government to expand a school facing severe space constraints. It has also led to initiatives such as Mahiti Mitras (information and service centres) that help people access rights and government schemes, women’s self-help groups (Sakhi Sanginis), and greater participation of women and girls in decision-making. Other efforts include resident-led affordable housing, restoration of a polluted wetland for safe water access, moves towards water self-sufficiency in a dry region, and the development of a ward-level Biodiversity Management Plan._2

Cooperation Jackson has created cooperative institutions through which workers and residents generate dignified livelihoods in an urban context. A cooperative is an autonomous association of people who come together to meet shared economic, social, and cultural needs through a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise. These include a lawn care business, an organic farm, and a print shop, along with a cooperative incubator and a community land trust. Cooperatives in construction, housing, and waste management are also envisioned. Together, these initiatives address poverty and discrimination while remaining ecologically sensitive, and connect with wider movements challenging capitalism, racism, and other structures of domination._2

This initiative has attempted to bring the true spirit of democracy alive in an urban context, wherein the currently dominant system makes most of the decisions in a highly centralized, bureaucratic, and top-down fashion. Typically, such top-down and elite-captured governance is at the cost of marginalized communities, who do not have much voice. This initiative gave voice to the people in the decision-making, leading to positive changes across many dimensions, such as gender equality, meeting basic needs such as water, housing, etc, and conservation of biodiversity. HIC has shown that in urban areas, all power need not be concentrated in elected politicians (corporators) and the bureaucrats they appoint, or in so-called 'expert' institutions, but that people can claim collective power to provide for themselves, as also make official agencies accountable._2

In direct contrast to dominant systems that promote individualisation, selfishness, dependence on markets and governments, and hostile competition, Cooperation Jackson is based on values of self-help, self-responsibility, care, democracy, equality, equity, and solidarity. Members believe in honesty, openness, social responsibility, and care for others. They reinvest most of their surpluses into job creation, community development, and a social security system. The shift is from ‘I, me, mine’ to ‘We, us, ours’, without erasing individual identities. This extends to solidarity with oppressed peoples elsewhere, including raising funds for a greenhouse project in Palestine._2

While the initiative led to many positive outcomes, challenges remained. Some corporators were less invested in their wards, and it was often difficult to sustain regular participation in Area Committee meetings beyond annual planning. Discussions tended to focus on immediate, local concerns rather than a broader vision for the wards. Meetings also prioritised infrastructure issues such as water and sanitation, while “softer” concerns like education, livelihoods, and mobility received less attention. This reflects a long-standing discourse that frames development primarily in terms of physical infrastructure rather than social transformation._2

Cooperation Jackson shows us that it is possible to move towards dignity and humane living even in the face of intense exploitation and inequality. To do this, several factors are crucial: coming together as collectives, enabling the voice and agency of the marginalised, dreaming alternative futures with feet firmly rooted on the ground, networking with other movements, and trying new approaches knowing that some may fail. It is also important to have diverse activities such as practical economic activities, dialogues and workshops, events of mutual aid and care, celebratory events including art, music and festivals, demonstrations and solidarity protests, and more. Finally, Cooperation Jackson also displays the necessity of networking with other movements and groups across the region and globally, for cross-learning and collective strength._2

This initiative shows that when citizens and CSOs come together, they can create a deeper and more holistic form of democracy, with communities at the centre of decision-making and representatives accountable to their needs. It brings local knowledge, innovation, and agency to the forefront rather than marginalising them. It also demonstrates that with the right opportunities, marginalised urban communities can assert themselves and move towards greater dignity and self-help. At a time of increasing centralisation, this offers hope for more decentralised forms of local governance in cities._2
Looking at lived examples helps us understand how alternatives emerge, take root, and grow through everyday practice and collective action._2

path.id: Direct and Delegated Democracy Decision making and power rooted in communities, collectives, exercised in form of care, interbeingness, community rights and responsibilities, and respect for and kinship with all of life._3
Ecological Integrity & Resilience Deep care for nature – protecting biodiversity, preserving ecological functions, and respecting the rights of all life, guided by ecological ethics in all actions._3

Economic Democracy An economy that cares for all people and the rest of nature, never pushing costs to peripheries (offshore, downstream, non-humans, future generations). Local economies, commons-based exchange, a shrinking owner–worker gap._3
Social Well-Being and Justice Focus on fulfilling lives for all. Equity across identities, community harmony, and dismantling hierarchies based on caste, gender, ability, class, or faith._3

Cultural Diversity and Knowledge Democracy Celebrating diverse ways ways of living and knowing – knowledge shared as commons, fostering innovation, creativity, and plural world-views, while sustaining cultural diversity in languages, foods, faiths, arts, and more._3
Commons as Knowledge, Creativity and Innovation Knowledge shared, co-created, and rooted in cultural memory — a space for collective learning, imagination, and solutions._3
Pluralism and Diversity Protecting cultural, ecological, and economic diversity as essential to resilience._3
